of Florida Levin College of Law</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Most of these people are incarcerated based on civil contempt, so they did not have access to a public defender,” Katz said. “That’s a problem in jurisdictions where courts have limited time and resources to dig in on whether the failure to pay is willful.”</p><p>“There’s a real risk,” she said, “that people are being incarcerated for reasons beyond their control and in a manner that is counterproductive.”</p><p>There are parallels to another legal process that’s drawn wide criticism: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/13/civil-asset-forfeiture-chicago-police-department-cook-county-property-seizures" target="_blank" >civil asset forfeiture</a>. People who face having their cars or cash forfeited because cops suspect the property was tied to a crime also don’t have an automatic right to an attorney.</p><p>In criminal courts, people accused of anything from shoplifting to murder have the right to a public defender if they don't have the money to pay a lawyer. Not so, though, in the civil court system.</p><p>Cook County has established a rule to connect low-income litigants in domestic relations cases with volunteer lawyers through bar associations when they face possible orders of indirect civil contempt for failing to pay their support. </p><p>But Monkus said those efforts have largely faltered. She said bar associations in Chicago are not recruiting lawyers to take cases involving involuntary civil contempt on a volunteer basis or maintaining comprehensive lists of attorneys available for appointment. Even when such lists existed, judges often did not rely on them, she said.</p><p>“It sounds like most of the judges were not making the appointments anyway,” Monkus said.</p><p>Chief Cook County Judge Charles S. Beach II didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>In 2017, Cook County created a program in which hearing officers assist self-represented litigants with navigating family court proceedings. But those hearing officers are prohibited from giving legal advice.</p><p>Monkus describes the program as “generally successful” but insufficient to address the broader lack of legal representation.</p><p>“There is the sense that a lot of the failure to pay could be prevented if the parent had representation earlier in the process,” she said.</p><p>Most of the contempt cases differ sharply from the highly publicized examples of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/10/09/deadbeat-dad-tycoon-applebees-restaurant-convicted-federal-court-evan-musikantow" target="_blank" ><u>wealthy parents failing to pay</u></a> large support judgments, advocates say.</p><p>“The issue is often, ‘Can I pay my rent versus can I pay my child support?’ ” Monkus said.</p><p>At the heart of whether someone is found in contempt for not paying is whether the failure to pay was “willful.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/4/30/23702915/video-charge-battery-fcook-county-jail-detainee" target="_blank" >Fanady</a> has been held in jail for indirect civil contempt of court since June 28, 2022. The Illinois appeals court found his incarceration was proper because he was able to turn over $10 million in stock awarded to his former wife.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div appeals court ordered Cerda’s release from jail, finding that Scannicchio failed to adequately determine whether Cerda had the financial ability to comply with the order.</p><p>“The trial court abused its discretion by ordering him jailed without making a finding that he had the ability to pay the purge amount,” the court said.</p><p>There's been no activity documented in the case since January 2025.</p><p>Cerda didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Some family courts have experimented with ways to divert parents from a course that might end with a contempt order and jail. "Parental accountability courts” have been operating in Georgia for 17 years. The aim is to help noncustodial parents find employment and job training and combat substance abuse so they can make a dent in their support debts without repeated contempt findings or jail stays. </p><p>According to state officials in Georgia, child-support collections have risen significantly after people “graduate” from these courts.</p><p>A similar accountability court in downstate Madison County was launched in 2016 — the first of its kind in Illinois. But it no longer exists in the county’s array of specialty courts. A court official there couldn’t explain why the court is no longer operating.</p><p>Katz said more study is needed to determine which approaches are most effective in helping parents meet their child-support obligations, especially in cases involving people who are barely scraping by.</p><p>“It’s incredibly hard to see how to fix the system,” she said. “The issue of how to financially support children with low-income parents has plagued courts and legislatures for over 100 years.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/4/30/23702915/video-charge-battery-fcook-county-jail-detainee" target="_blank" >Video appears to contradict charge of battery filed against a Cook County Jail detainee</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson to introduce measure to protect Chicago renters
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson plans to introduce a sweeping ordinance that aims to protect the city’s renters from eviction and predatory practices.</p><p>The “Protecting Renters Ordinance” seeks to update the city’s 40-year-old Residential Landlord Tenant Ordinance (RLTO), which oversees the legal rights and responsibilities of tenants and landlords.</p><p>The ordinance would also establish a rental registry, and create a new administrative body that works with renters and landlords to resolve disputes, among other measures.</p><p>Chicago’s Department of Housing Commissioner Lissette Castañeda said the proposal “[meets] the moment. Affordability is at the top of everyone's concerns, and we want to make sure that something that's been necessary for a long time can finally get done.”</p><p>City officials say the measure, which the mayor plans to introduce to the city’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate" >housing</a> committee next month, affects more than 600,000 renter households across Chicago,</p><p>According to a draft of the ordinance, updates to the RLTO include a ban on hidden junk fees, such as application and processing fees charged on top of rent, and require that any amounts charged to renters reflect actual, documented costs. It also establishes a Tenant Bill of Rights and requires landlords to disclose if they’re using <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/data/2024/10/22/chicagos-rental-crisis-is-an-algorithm-rigging-the-system?subscription=true" target="_blank" >algorithmic pricing</a> tools.</p><p>The ordinance would also create a rental registry, which housing advocates have sought for years. The city currently has no comprehensive record of its more than 500,000 rental units, nor does it keep a record of who owns the properties and whether they are complying with the law. In addition, more property owners are using limited liability companies, or LLCs, which can shield problem landlords from city enforcement and make it difficult for renters to address their living conditions, as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/housing/2025/09/05/chicago-landlords-renters-property-management-llc?subscription=true" target="_blank" >WBEZ reported last year</a>.</p><p>“It's very difficult to hold those who are doing wrong by their tenants accountable,” said Jung Yoon, the mayor’s chief of policy. “What the rental registry will help us do is not just know quickly whom to contact, but also to start tracking patterns and understanding trends” regarding building violations and speculation in gentrifying neighborhoods.</p><p>The rental registry, Yoon said, would require landlords to pay an annual fee, and the amount would be determined by building size and owner occupancy. Owner-occupied, two- to six-unit buildings and nonprofit affordable housing are exempt from the fee. Larger building owners would be charged anywhere from $20 to $60 a unit.</p><p>The annual fees, which the city expects could total around $20 million, would help fund the initiatives laid out in the bill, Yoon said. The funds would go toward improving inspections and enforcement.</p><p>The money would also establish the Bureau of Rental Housing Services, designed to be the city’s first coordinated hub for rental housing. The bureau would administer the rental registry, provide renters with emergency rental and relocation help, refer tenants to eviction prevention programs, provide compliance guidance for landlords and enforce tenant protections.</p><p>But some landlords and realtor groups are skeptical of the new proposal, arguing that these measures are burdensome and will ultimately drive up the cost of housing.</p><p>The measure “is putting in dozens of new requirements, obligations and costs to operate a building,” said Jeff Weinberg, founder and president of Drexel Properties, which owns 600 units and manages 85 buildings.</p><p>He is also on the executive committee of the Neighborhood Building Owners Alliance, a non-profit representing housing providers across the city.</p><p>Weinberg, who said 85% of his units are affordable, took issue with the annual rental registry fee. He also questioned the “Just Cause for Eviction" provision of the ordinance, which in part requires landlords to pay relocation assistance to tenants in a no-fault eviction, such as when rehabbing the property, converting to condos or demolition.</p><p>“You have to pay people to move out, you have to pay a registry,” he said. “That is not solving the problem. The real problem that we have is a [housing] supply issue.”</p><p>Tom Benedetto, who represents the Chicago Association of Realtors, said half of the group’s members are housing providers. He said the ordinance would “make more neighborhood-focused housing providers think twice about investing in their community and maybe getting out of the business altogether.” Benedetto said that opens the door to larger corporations and investors.</p><p>But housing advocates said these criticisms of the mayor’s proposal are old.</p><p>“Landlords and real estate interests very often use the argument that any regulation will increase costs,” said Jonah Karsh, a housing organizer with the Metropolitan Tenants Organization.</p><p>Karsh said the rental landscape has changed in the past few decades.</p><p>“A lot more of our housing stock is owned by corporations or people that are owning the property as an investment property rather than one that they live in themselves,” Karsh said.</p><p>He added that many cities — including New York City, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, and north suburban Evanston — already have policies similar to those the mayor is proposing.</p><p>Roderick Wilson, with affordable housing advocacy organization Lugenia Burns Hope Center, said the proposed ordinance is a collection of tenant protections that housing advocates have been demanding for years.</p><p>He added that the real estate lobby argues that “mom-and-pop landlords” would be overly penalized by any regulations or fees, but he said the proposed ordinance provides exemptions for such property owners.</p><p>Wilson hopes Chicagoans, more than half of whom are renters, will encourage their Council representatives to vote for the measure — especially amid the tight housing market and challenging economic conditions.</p><p>“It’s hard out here for folks — you have landlords raising rents, maintenance of buildings not being up to speed, a high increase in folks being evicted,” he said. “This [proposal] is a step in the right direction.”</p>

entries.title: Portage Park man's tattoo honors four years of sobriety
entries.summary: <p>For Steven Bruehl, quitting drinking felt like getting glasses for the first time: Life became sharper. He found himself noticing small things, like the leaves on the trees. He can’t imagine going back to how things were before.</p><p>“I saw joy in everyday things,” he said. “I had never experienced that joy.” </p><p>Bruehl, 54, was in active addiction for around seven years before he took his last drink and checked himself in for intensive outpatient treatment in April 2022. Four years later, he looks at a new tattoo on his forearm and sees a reminder of his recovery.</p><p>The tattoo is a heart shape filled with flowers, mushrooms and skulls that symbolize different parts of his life and his experience of recovery.</p><p>The tattoo is a celebration of his sobriety, but he doesn’t shy away from the dark moments that preceded his revamped life. Sitting in tattoo artist Orlando Camacho’s chair, tattoo needle buzzing and permanently inscribing his skin the day after his four-year anniversary of being sober in April, Bruehl reflected on the reality of his day-to-day life during active addiction.</p><p>“It's not the actual being drunk or passing out or getting to a point where you can't talk or whatever,” he said. “That's part of it. But the amount of time you think about, ‘When am I gonna go get it? How am I gonna get it? Where am I gonna hide it? Am I gonna hide it?’ It is all consuming.”</p><p>For years before he admitted he needed help, Bruehl says he was in denial. He thought of his stable career, his master’s degrees, his generally successful life, and convinced himself he didn’t have a problem. But before he knew it, he was drinking every day.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Steven Bruehl’s tattoo is a heart shape filled with flowers, mushrooms and skulls that symbolize different parts of his life and his experience of recovery.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Bruehl’s husband, Cesar Barradas, knew Bruehl needed to quit drinking long before he did. Desperate for a change, Barradas collected empty liquor bottles and left notes on half-drank ones begging Bruehl to stop, to choose their relationship, to get help.</p><p>In 2022, Bruehl’s drinking reached a new level. It was affecting his whole life. Bruehl was passed out at home one day when he finally said the words out loud.</p><p>“I was calling his therapist and going, ‘We need to do something,’” Barradas said.</p><p>Bruehl reflects on that moment as near rock-bottom.</p><p>“I got off the elevator in the basement, but not maybe quite all the way down,” he said.</p><p>Days later, Bruehl went downtown to the Positive Sobriety Institute and enrolled in its intensive outpatient treatment program.</p><p>He recalls listening to different people tell their stories of addiction, and he related to many of them, even the scary ones. There were times he should have been hospitalized, he said.</p><p>He took a leave of absence from his work as a middle school Chicago Public Schools teacher and attended eight hours of therapy every day for six weeks.</p><p>There, he found a community of supporters, inspirations and peers to commiserate with, share advice and lean on through his sobriety.</p><p>“You think you've told your partner everything in life and your family, and you think you told your friends everything,” Bruehl said. “No, these people, five or six people in this small group I was with for about six weeks, know absolutely every horrible thing.”</p><p>It’s hard for Bruehl to put a finger on exactly what made him addicted to alcohol. There’s certainly the genetic component, and he also suspects part of him was trying to push his problems and emotions aside in pursuit of helping others. He always wanted to appear OK, and disregarding his emotions led to him using alcohol as a comfort, he said.</p><p>Barradas had watched Bruehl slip into addiction and begged him to get help, but looking back, he now knows it always had to come from him; no one else could make him stop drinking. Getting to treatment was a huge step, but it was just the first step, Barradas said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It's relief, but it's also uncertainty,” Barradas said. “It's just starting. It's day one. Is there gonna be a day 10?”</p><p>Four years after Bruehl’s last drink, life looks a lot different. He enjoys vacations in a way he never did before. His memories of beautiful places are sharp and clear instead of fogged by alcohol, overshadowed by the constant pursuit of his next drink or completely gone.</p><p>“We spent 10 grand to go to Barcelona,” he said. “And I don't remember what I saw. I mean, what a waste of an opportunity to see some stuff.”</p><p>And, for the first time since before he slipped into addiction, he finds himself bored, asking himself: “What do I do with all this time?” He was used to his time and mental space being taken up by drinking. But it was in that boredom that he found a new mindset, a new way to approach life that he had never tapped into before.</p><p>“It's really hard to put into words, like there's this freedom, this joy, this love of life that I really didn't have,” he said.</p><p>He wanted something permanent to commemorate his sobriety and recognize how far he'd come. Once he decided on a tattoo, he knew Camacho was the right artist for the job. Camacho is Barradas’ cousin and had gotten to know Bruehl over the years. He had done some other tattoos for Bruehl, including a bright red cardinal and an outline of the state of Minnesota with trees and a loon drawn inside.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-020000" name="image-020000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6ea8814/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7694x4318+0+407/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd9%2F74%2Fd74109ad4381a456b37f1ac2a0bd%2Fsobrietytattoo-2604120320.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bb3f200/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7694x4318+0+407/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd9%2F74%2Fd74109ad4381a456b37f1ac2a0bd%2Fsobrietytattoo-2604120320.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b67fe49/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7694x4318+0+407/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd9%2F74%2Fd74109ad4381a456b37f1ac2a0bd%2Fsobrietytattoo-2604120320.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Tattoo artist Orlando Camacho is a cousin of Steven Bruehl's partner, Cesar Barradas. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b67fe49/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7694x4318+0+407/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd9%2F74%2Fd74109ad4381a456b37f1ac2a0bd%2Fsobrietytattoo-2604120320.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7db5dfa/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7694x4318+0+407/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd9%2F74%2Fd74109ad4381a456b37f1ac2a0bd%2Fsobrietytattoo-2604120320.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b67fe49/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7694x4318+0+407/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd9%2F74%2Fd74109ad4381a456b37f1ac2a0bd%2Fsobrietytattoo-2604120320.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Tattoo artist Orlando Camacho is a cousin of Steven Bruehl’s partner, Cesar Barradas. Camacho applied Bruehl’s tattoo in a four-hour session.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The two worked together on the design. Camacho, who owns the Tattoo Art Collective in Highwood, considered what he knew about Bruehl when putting the tattoo design together. The final design included Camacho’s signature skulls and mushrooms because they “grow out of the muck,” symbolizing Bruehl finding sobriety. Camacho also added Barradas’ birth flower.</p><p>“Even though I did horrible things, I don't have to claim those things for the rest of my life,” Bruehl said.</p><p>For Camacho, doing tattoos for family and friends is an honor, but it comes with a level of pressure that tattooing strangers doesn’t.</p><p>“I'll probably see them at a family function, or I'll see them at a barbecue,” Camacho said. “And people that I know very dearly will see that tattoo. And so you want to do even better.”</p><p>Watching Camacho work diligently on the tattoo, Barradas thought about how far he and Bruehl had come.</p><p>“He's always been so caring, he's been the guru of his family, always bringing people together,” Barradas said. “It was there before, during the toughest years of him drinking, it was still there, but now it's just freer.”</p><div entries.summary: <p>"Go home Jerome!"</p><p>Those three words are found at the bottom of a West Town mural that looks like a booking photo. A little dude with glasses, flyaway black hair and massive chompers poses with a big, cheesy smile. His eyes are closed and he’s flashing the peace sign while holding another sign saying “Chicago Police Dept.” and "18 Aug. 2025."</p><p>Tucked in his pocket is the criminal evidence: a can of spray paint.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1e0000" name="image-1e0000"></a> <picture data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Artist Jerome Tiunayan stands across the alley from the Little Jerome mural with another mural, one that he painted with his friend and fellow Chicago muralist, Birdmilk.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Jerome is the childlike alter ego of muralist Jerome Tiunayan of Little Village. He was inspired by Calvin of Calvin and Hobbes, the comic strip by Bill Watterson that Tiunayan says he's loved since he was a kid.</p><p>“It’s me trying to throw my hat into that ring,” Tiunayan says. “I’ve always wanted to have a character like that and send him off to adventures.”</p><p>Little Jerome’s booking portrait is in an alley off North Greenview Avenue, between West Chicago Avenue and West Fry Street. Across the alley, Jerome makes another appearance in a mural that Tiunayan painted with his friend and fellow Chicago muralist, Birdmilk.</p><p>But little Jerome is mainly found in Tiunayan’s studio art, where he draws freehand with acrylic paint on canvas or panel. There little Jerome strikes a pose in front of a mirror, rock climbs over a river, rushes to school, meditates under a waterfall and daydreams about being a boxer, among other adventures.</p><p>It’s “easier to communicate certain emotions and ideas … through the lens of a child,” Tiunayan says. Painting Little Jerome is a way of making his art autobiographical without being heavy handed.</p><p>For the booking photo mural, Tiunayan says he used mainly spray paint and finished the detail work with a brush. The piece was commissioned by the building owner, who wanted to communicate the different impressions many have of street art. Is it graffiti? Is it celebrated? Is it a crime?</p><p>For the mural he came up with “this innocent little kid, wet behind the ears, juxtaposing it with a mug shot,” Tiunayan says.</p><p>Tiunayan and his wife, a Chicago Public Schools teacher, moved to Chicago about three years ago from Brooklyn where Tiunayan was born and raised, he says.</p><p>The handle “Go Home Jerome!” was concocted for Tiunayan’s first Twitter profile in high school.</p><p>Along with painting little Jerome, Tiunayan says he works at “anything that keeps me in the studio.” That could be digital design, freelance work, communications, tattoo designs or art installations.</p><p>Tiunayan’s work also can be found at Chicago’s Vertical Gallery, which specializes in touring exhibits of urban-contemporary art, as well as his website.</p><p>“This life is very uncertain,” Tiunayan says of being an artist. “I’ll take on anything that comes my way.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d00000" name="module-d00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Murals and Mosaics Newsletter</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-990000" name="html-embed-module-990000"></a><div class="piano-sidebar-newsletter-murals-and-mosaics"></div> </div> </div></div> </div><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b20000" name="module-b20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Chicago’s murals and mosaics sidebar</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics" target="_blank" >Chicago’s murals & mosaics</a></h3>Part of a series on public art in the city and suburbs. <b>Know of a mural or mosaic? Tell us where, and email a photo to </b><a class="Link" href="mailto:murals@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><b><i>murals@suntimes.com</i></b></a><b>. </b>We might do a story on it.<br></div> </div><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d80000" name="html-embed-module-d80000"></a><div class="flourish-embed" data-src="visualisation/629878"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script></div> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Red Line subway closing for first of four weekends of repairs
entries.summary: <p>Red Line trains will be rerouted to elevated tracks for the whole weekend — the first of four weekend detours needed for maintenance work in the Loop subway, according to the CTA.</p><p>The detour will last from 10 p.m. Friday to 4 a.m. Monday. Red Line trains will be rerouted from the Fullerton to Cermak-Chinatown stations.</p><p>For the length of the detour, trains will not stop at these stations: North/Clybourn, Clark/Division, Chicago, Grand, Lake, Monroe, Jackson, Harrison and Roosevelt. Instead, trains will stop at Brown Line stops including Amitage, Sedgwick, Merchandise Mart, Clark/Lake, Washington/Wabash, Adams/Wabash, and the elevated tracks at the Roosevelt station.</p><div entries.title: Here’s what Chicagoans would tell hometown pontiff Pope Leo XIV
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson on Thursday became the latest Illinois politician to made the trek to Vatican City to meet with Dolton-born Pope Leo XIV. While Johnson spent about an hour with the pontiff discussing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/05/28/mayor-brandon-johnson-pope-leo-vatican-visit-meeting" >war, affordability and the legacy of slavery</a>, we wanted to know what you would ask the pope if you had his ear for five minutes.</p><p>"I'd want to know his feelings on the separation of church and state — and does he have a good sense of humor?" <i>— Paul Lockwood</i></p><p>"As an American, what additional pressure, if any, do you feel to remain true to God’s word and truth — even when it conflicts [and] collides with the trending downward of America’s current value system?" <i>— Derek D. Forest</i></p><p>"How did he start and continue to question AI?" — <i>John Dunn Smith</i></p><p>"I would ask the Pope that if the earth is a gift from God, what responsibilities do we have as caretakers for its viability?" — <i>Joe</i></p><p>"The Church's poor treatment of survivors of abuse by clergy/religious and — by contrast — the empathy and compassion that they show to abusers." <i>— Terry Steubenville</i></p><p>"If he ever hung out at Orland Park's mall like I did." <i>— Jennifer Bronson Jackson</i></p><p>"I would ask Pope Leo about his early years in Chicago’s south suburbs. I’m especially curious about the people who really shaped him and the important moments, even seemingly inconsequential ones, that led him to his current path." <i>— Janet Volk</i></p><p>"When will the church permit women to become priests?" — <i>Brian Piper</i></p><p>"Why do [Archdiocese of Chicago] Cardinal [Blase] Cupich and COO Betsy Bohlen appear to view Catholic education no longer as a sacred mission, but merely as a financial line item? With more than $500 million in liquid assets, why are schools being closed over relatively modest annual deficits of $140,000 — shortfalls that could likely be resolved through better management, stronger oversight and a renewed commitment to the Church’s educational mission?" — <i>Angel Garcia</i></p><p>"I would let His Holiness know that it was so very neat (and appropriate) that he quoted J.R.R. Tolkien (LOTR, Return of the King) in his first Encyclical. He is truly a Mellon [<a class="Link" href="https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Mellon" target="_blank" >friend</a>]." — <i>tpturneriv</i></p><p>"I'll ask him what are his greatest concerns, and we'll pray over it." <i>— Angel Pia Jr.</i></p><p>"I would ask if and when he plans to come back to visit Chicago." — <i>Chris Devine</i></p><p>"How 'bout those Sox!" <i>— Daniel Novik</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-970000" name="module-970000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Mayor Brandon Johnson meets Pope Leo XIV</h3>The Chicago mayor is visiting Rome this week as part of a multi-faith delegation to the pontiff. Johnson had a private audience with Leo on Thursday afternoon Central European time.<br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-471167b2-5aa6-11f1-807d-6fa3a0429666"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/05/28/mayor-brandon-johnson-pope-leo-vatican-visit-meeting" >Mayor Johnson, Pope Leo talk slavery, wars and a Chicago invitation during historic Vatican visit</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/05/28/mayor-brandon-johnson-pope-leo-vatican-visit-meeting" >Gifts for Pope Leo XIV range from lavish to local favorites: ‘What to get someone who has everything?’</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/05/28/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-vatican-visit-pope-leo-faith-spirituality" >Ahead of meeting Pope Leo, Johnson speaks of ‘evolving’ spirituality and ‘constantly growing in my faith’</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/05/28/mayor-brandon-johnson-delegation-trip-visit-pope-leo-xiv-rome" >Here’s who’s with Mayor Brandon Johnson on his trip to visit Pope Leo XIV in Rome</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2026/05/25/pope-leo-calls-for-robust-regulation-of-ai-in-manifesto-that-ponders-the-future-of-humanity" >Pope Leo calls for robust regulation of AI in manifesto that ponders the future of humanity</a></li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Ooh la la, Chicago to install high-fashion French lawn chairs beside Buckingham Fountain
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Park District will debut 100 green metal chairs around Buckingham Fountain Saturday as part of a new pilot program that takes a cue from European cities like Paris and encourages people to socialize in the lakefront park.</p><p>But having somewhere to sit comes with a price tag.</p><p>The 100 chairs, which were manufactured by the brand Fermob in Paris, cost $54,438 in total, according to a Park District spokesperson. Of that, $24,438 was footed by the city. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lollapalooza/2026/05/12/lollapalooza-schedule" target="_blank" ><u>Lollapalooza,</u></a> which partnered on the project and will host its 21st festival in Grant Park July 30-Aug. 2, paid the remaining $30,000.</p><p>In a statement, the Park District said, “the seating program will transform the space and encourage social gathering.” The movable chairs will be in the park until September, except, the city says, during major events hosted in Grant Park, although it did not specify which events would prompt chair removal.</p><p>The selection of these specific chairs was inspired by the seating in Paris’ Luxembourg Garden, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoparkdistrict.com/buckingham-fountain-chairs" target="_blank" ><u>city announcement</u></a>. In Chicago, 50 of the chairs will have an upright back and 50 will be slightly reclined.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-9d0000" name="html-embed-module-9d0000"></a><iframe src="https://www.facebook.com/plugins/video.php?height=476&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.facebook.com%2Freel%2F1649178776357979%2F&show_text=false&width=267&t=0" width="267" height="476" style="border:none;overflow:hidden" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen="true" allow="autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; picture-in-picture; web-share" allowFullScreen="true"></iframe> </div> </div><p>In Paris, the same style of chairs have been a fixture for more than a century, and they’ve been designed by Fermob since 2004. Online retailers sell the upright Fermob Luxembourg chairs in a variety of colors for $500 a piece. The low armchairs run more than $1,000 each. (The chairs are so trendy that a <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DVbD1pZDddH/?utm_source=ig_web_button_share_sheet" target="_blank" ><u>miniaturized version</u></a> recently served as the invite to Dior’s runway show during Paris Fashion Week.)</p><p>Buckingham Fountain, which was turned on for the season <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/05/09/buckingham-fountain-switched-on-for-2026-summer-season" target="_blank" ><u>in early May</u></a>, runs for 20 minutes every hour, during which a center jet shoots as high as 150 feet into the air. The display begins daily at 9 a.m. The new chairs will be secured each evening after the last fountain display at 11 p.m., according to the Park District.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>People lounge in the iconic green chairs in Paris’ Luxembourg Garden. The Chicago Park District said similar chairs will “bring a piece of France to Chicago’s Front Yard.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jacques Brinon/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>While the fountain is undoubtedly one of the city’s most iconic landmarks, the lack of seating nearby has been the subject of local chatter for years. Back in 2022, Chicagoan Rick Weber set off a conversation on Twitter when he posted about what he observed one day near the fountain: Visitors taking their photo and then leaving, since there was nowhere to sit and the nearby food stands were closed.</p><p>On WBEZ’s talk show, Reset, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/reset-with-sasha-ann-simons/2022/05/24/why-arent-chicagos-public-spaces-more-like-europes" target="_blank" ><u>Weber and other guests talked about</u></a> how Chicago ought to make public parks more aligned with those in places like Paris. “This is supposed to be the front porch of Chicago, right?” Weber said at the time. “So, what sort of hospitality do we extend not only to our own citizens but to people who are visiting here?”</p><p>Now, the city has rolled out a plan years in the making. The 100 chairs debuting this weekend are part of a larger initiative, called “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoparkdistrict.com/featured-capital-projects#132756" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago’s Front Yard Reimagined 2026</u></a>,” which was published in February as an update to a 2002 plan. One of the new plan’s most ambitious ideas would move DuSable Lake Shore Drive below ground for a stretch and extend Buckingham Fountain’s surrounding landscaping all the way to the lakefront.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: Malört aims to set world record for largest-ever group taking shots of the spirit
entries.summary: <p>Malört hopes to set the world record Sunday for the largest group of people taking a shot of Malört at the same time, the company announced.</p><p>The event, titled “Bad Decision for Good Cause,” is scheduled for 7:30 pm at Recess on 838 W. Kinzie St on Aug. 30 from 5-9 p.m. It will double as a charity fundraiser for Ravenswood Community Services, a Chicago nonprofit that provides food, housing, and supportive services for those in the city facing homelessness.</p><p>Tickets cost $12. The admission price includes that one shot of Malört needed to make that world record attempt. CH Distillery of Chicago, the makers of Jeppson's Malört, said it will match every ticket purchase with a $10 donation to the nonprofit.</p><p>"Malört brings people together for the shared experience of a questionable choice,” Tremaine Atkinson, CEO of CH Distillery, said in a news release. “This event is the perfect way to gather and give back to a great cause while we’re at it. We’re going to attempt something patently ridiculous and do some serious good for Chicago in the process.”</p><p>Non-drinkers also are encouraged to purchase a $12 ticket to enjoy live entertainment, food and to watch the making of what Malört hopes will be a new world record.</p>

>Bears stadium bill, state budget unresolved as Springfield session winds down</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whtlhn-l-s/" target="_blank" >Mitchell number of key measures hanging in the balance as the state constitutional deadline of midnight Sunday nears.</p><p><b>'Megaprojects' bill</b>: The effort to advance property tax incentive legislation to help the Bears build a new stadium in Arlington Heights remains ongoing. target="_blank" >Fathom opens as part of couple’s planned mini empire of queer-focused bars</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whtlhn-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Maggie Hennessy</a></h5><p>When Fathom, the nautical-lite queer neighborhood bar in Lake View, debuted in early April, it became the first official joint project of married business partners Whitney LaMora and Zoe Schor.</p><p>Between real estate negotiations, fundraising, buildouts, hiring and permitting, it took 2.5 years for LaMora and Schor to open Fathom after their first glimpse of 1622 W. Belmont Ave., formerly Flagship Tavern. </p><p>The couple, who also own the subterranean lesbian cocktail lounge Dorothy Downstairs in West Town, have higher ambitions that stretch beyond Chicago as they build the city’s first lesbian-owned hospitality group solely focused on creating queer gathering places.</p><p>"My wife never stops looking for real estate," LaMora said of Schor. "She’s always hungry for the next project."</p><p>So far, their business venture — called Friend of Dorothy Bars — is backed by 30 mostly local investors who’ve bought into their vision, too.</p><p>"We are really showing that the queer community wants and deserves these beautiful spaces," LaMora said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whtlhn-l-tu/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Do you remember the first time you went to the lakefront in Chicago? Tell us about it.</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply with your answer here to this</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whtlhn-l-ir/" target="_blank" >What would you bring the pope?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said…</p><p>"A big can of Garrett Mix popcorn!  A delicious taste of home for Pope Leo!" — <i>Janet Volk</i></p><p>"A very wet Italian beef sandwich from Tony’s on Pulaski." — <i>Maria Rose Therese</i></p><p>"Celery salt for his Chicago-style hot dogs. I'm sure it's hard to find in Italy." — <i>Tony Galati</i></p><p>"A miniature replica of Holy Name Cathedral because it is a beautiful Chicago landmark." — <i>Bonnie Collins</i></p><p>"A bottle of Malört." — <i>Anshul Jain</i></p><hr><p></p><h4>ONE MORE THING 🔊</h4><p>Vocalo, WBEZ's sister radio station for music, is <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whtlhn-l-iy/" target="_blank" >premiering a new call-in request show tonight at 8 p.m.</a> </p><p>Hosted by Vocalo DJ Nudia Hernandez, The Vocalo Hotline show will air weekly on WBEZ 91.5 FM and Vocalo 91.1 FM. Listeners can call in with their shout-outs, messages and dedications paired with a song. </p><p>You can listen live via the WBEZ app or <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whtlhn-l-ij/" target="_blank" >online here</a>.</p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you.Become a member to make stories like these free and available to everyone. Learn more at </i><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whtlhn-l-it/" target="_blank" ><i>suntimes.com/member</i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: Familia de Adam Toledo presenta nueva demanda contra oficial de la Policía de Chicago que le disparó fatalmente
entries.summary: <p>La familia de Adam Toledo presentó esta semana una nueva demanda contra la Ciudad de Chicago y el oficial de policía que disparó fatalmente al adolescente de 13 años.</p><p>El caso fue presentado un mes después de que la familia <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/17/adam-toledo-lawsuit-dropped-cpd-officer" target="_blank" >retirara abruptamente otra demanda</a> presentada en la corte del Condado de Cook, justo días antes de que comenzaran los argumentos de apertura. Ahora, el proceso legal comenzará nuevamente ante la corte federal, más de cinco años después de que Toledo fuera asesinado.</p><p>“Ultimadamente, buscamos transparencia, responsabilidad y la protección de todos los derechos constitucionales del demandante”, afirmó la abogada de la familia, Adeena Weiss Ortiz, al Sun-Times.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f00000" name="module-f00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En el juicio previamente programado, un juez del Condado de Cook accedió a la solicitud de la Municipalidad de dividir la demanda inicial, exigiendo que el abogado de la familia primero comprobara las acusaciones relacionadas con el tiroteo antes de pasar a sus afirmaciones de que la Municipalidad fue negligente al contratar a Eric Stillman, el oficial que le disparó a Toledo.</p><p>Weiss Ortiz dijo que creía que los dos casos estaban "intrínsecamente entrelazados", lo que la llevó a retirar el caso y volver a presentarlo a principios de esta semana en la Corte del Distrito de EE.UU. “Queríamos tener la oportunidad de presentar todas las reclamaciones que la familia tenía”, comentó.</p><p>Los abogados de la ciudad no comentan sobre litigios pendientes, pero anteriormente habían afirmado que la Municipalidad se defenderá de las acusaciones.</p><p>En marzo de 2021, Stillman persiguió a Toledo en un callejón de La Villita y le <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2021/4/1/22362227/adam-toledo-little-village-police-shooting" target="_blank" >disparó un tiro</a>segundos después de que el niño dejara caer una pistola y <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2021/4/16/22388070/el-video-del-tiroteo-fatal-contra-adam-toledo-detalla-los-ultimos-minutos-de-la-vida-del-nino" target="_blank" >levantara sus manos</a>.</p><p>La nueva demanda alega que Stillman violó el entrenamiento, las órdenes y las directivas del departamento al perseguir y dispararle fatalmente a Toledo. La queja también argumenta que la Municipalidad es responsable de contratar y retener a Stillman, a pesar de errores en su solicitud y problemas de salud en curso.</p><p>La Oficina Civil de Responsabilidad Policial (COPA) recomendó que se despidiera a Stillman, tras determinar que "actuó de manera inconsistente" con la capacitación del departamento sobre persecuciones a pie y usó fuerza letal de manera inapropiada.</p><p>Pero el caso disciplinario de Stillman se ha estancado debido a una batalla legal de años entre la Municipalidad y el mayor sindicato de policía de Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/09/16/chicago-police-union-fop-misconduct-discipline" target="_blank" >sobre el manejo de casos de mala conducta grave</a>.</p><p>El abogado de Stillman, Tim Grace, no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios. Anteriormente había dicho que consideraba que el retiro voluntario del caso del condado era un reconocimiento de que el uso de la fuerza por parte de Stillman estaba “dentro de la política y era razonable”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Estudiante de Chicago se vuelve a poner sus tacos de fútbol tras pasar meses detenido por inmigración
entries.summary: <p>Cuando Ricardo Navarrete corre con un balón de fútbol a sus pies, el mundo se detiene.</p><p>Pero durante más de dos meses, el estudiante de último año de la Secundaria Mather no tuvo esa escapatoria.</p><p>Desde marzo, ha estado atrapado en instalaciones de detención abarrotadas, con apenas espacio suficiente para hacer lagartijas, después de que oficiales de inmigración federales lo arrestaron a él y a su madre, Liliana Navarrete, durante una audiencia rutinaria de su caso de asilo.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a20000" name="module-a20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Ricardo se perdió muchas cosas. Semanas de su temporada de fútbol en el club. El baile de graduación. Y hasta esta semana, parecía que no podría caminar sobre el escenario de graduación de Mather. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/27/estudiante-de-cps-regresa-junto-a-su-madre-en-chicago-tras-ser-liberado-de-detencion-migratoria" target="_blank" >Ricardo fue liberado el martes</a> después de que una comunidad de defensores atrajo la atención nacional sobre la difícil situación de la familia y de que abogados lucharon por ellos en la corte. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/20/juez-ordena-la-liberacion-de-una-mama-de-cps-detenida-por-ice-su-hijo-adolescente-sigue-detenido" target="_blank" >Su mamá fue liberada la semana pasada</a>.</p><p>Y el miércoles, Ricardo finalmente volvió a ser un estudiante de secundaria, compitiendo en su primer partido de fútbol desde su detención. Aunque su equipo perdió y Ricardo fue duro consigo mismo respecto a su rendimiento, el joven de 18 años estaba encantado de estar de vuelta en el campo un día antes de recibir su diploma.</p><p>“Siento tantos sentimientos”, dijo Ricardo. “Estoy tan feliz de estar aquí. Sólo quiero estar con mi familia y jugar fútbol”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Se cortó el cabello.</p><p>Steven Navarrete, el hermano mayor de Ricardo, dijo que se puso feliz cuando se despertó y vio a Ricardo durmiendo en el sofá después de dos largos meses.</p><p>“Él está de regreso a donde se supone que debería estar”, dijo Steven.</p><p>Steven y Liliana observaron cómo Ricardo se calzaba sus zapatos de fútbol Saprix el miércoles, una marca colombiana que demuestra un pedazo de casa. Se preparaba para jugar al futsal, una variante del fútbol con equipos y campos más pequeños.</p><p>La multitud, animando desde la cerca de malla que rodea el campo de juego, casi explota cuando Ricardo pasó a los defensores y lanzó un potente disparo. Pero el balón se estrelló contra el poste de la portería.</p><p>Aun así, esas son algunas de las habilidades que Ricardo espera lucir el próximo año en Truman College, la potencia del fútbol de la class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Familiares y amigos acudieron a apoyar a Ricardo Navarrete mientras jugaba su primer partido de fútbol el miércoles desde que fue detenido.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Mateo Abrego, uno de los amigos más cercanos de Ricardo, estuvo allí para apoyarlo. Antes de ese día, Mateo había recogido la toga y el birrete de graduación de Ricardo. Aquellas semanas sin su amigo se sintió “triste, deprimido y solo”, dijo.</p><p>El primer vistazo que tuvo Mateo de Ricardo tras su liberación fue una sorpresa. Estaba en clase cuando un compañero le pasó un celular. Allí, en FaceTime, estaba su amigo.</p><p>“Lo único que dije fue ‘¡Wow, ese es Ricardo!’”, comentó Mateo. Gritó tan fuerte que casi tuvo problemas con su maestro.</p><p>Volver a ver a Ricardo ha sido un alivio para sus amigos y el personal de Mather, pero la campaña continua de deportaciones masivas de Trump sigue pesando en la mente de los maestros. A medida que se acerca el receso de verano, Vázquez dijo que le preocupa si algunos estudiantes tendrán suficiente para comer y si los agentes de inmigración tendrán una presencia más visible a medida que más personas salgan a disfrutar del clima cálido.</p><p>A veces, las crisis que enfrentan los estudiantes pueden resultar abrumadoras.</p><p>“Necesito tomarme un tiempo para desconectarme”, dijo Vázquez. “Pero, ¿qué pasa si no reviso mi correo electrónico durante una semana? ¿Pasará algo catastrófico? ¿Y pude haber hecho algo? Es increíblemente estresante”.</p><p>Kristy Morrow, una amiga de Ricardo y familia de Liliana que ayudó a recaudar fondos para cubrir sus gastos legales, dijo que ahora que están en casa intentará crear conciencia sobre otros en situaciones similares.</p><p>Cree que la atención y los esfuerzos comunitarios ayudaron a la familia, señalando que el senador estadounidense Dick Durbin, quien ha abogado durante mucho tiempo por reformas al sistema de inmigración del país, habló sobre el caso de Ricardo <a class="Link" href="https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/press/dem/releases/durbin-calls-for-release-of-chicago-high-school-senior-currently-detained-by-ice-despite-his-pending-asylum-case-and-lack-of-criminal-record" target="_blank" >en el Senado la semana pasada.</a></p><p>“Sabemos cuántas personas están detenidas en [los centros de] ICE y creo que la atención que recibimos fue fundamental para asegurar su liberación”, dijo Morrow. “Sin eso, no creo que hubiéramos tenido una oportunidad”.</p><p>La odisea de la familia aún no ha terminado. Continuarán su caso de asilo en la corte. Ricardo tiene que conectarse diariamente con ICE mediante un rastreador GPS que lleva en su muñeca. Después de su experiencia, Ricardo dijo que no le molesta demasiado.</p><p>“Entre estar allí, encerrado, y estar aquí, prefiero esto”, dijo Ricardo.</p><p>Por ahora, está feliz de recuperar el tiempo perdido.</p><p>Después de su juego, Ricardo se sentó con su familia y Mateo en una banca, disfrutando del brillante sol de la tarde en Chicago.</p><p><i>Contribuyó Sarah Karp. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Patients, doctors hail 'revolutionary' new drug for pancreatic cancer
entries.summary: <p>Last summer, Megan Chung was given one more year to live.</p><p>Chung, a mother of three college-age kids from Hinsdale, was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in April 2024. The disease — one of the most devastating and deadly cancers that kills roughly 50,000 people in the United States every year — already was advanced, and an inoperable tumor was crushing her intestines. </p><p>"When you're diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, 'I'm really sorry' is the first thing your doctor says," said Chung, 55.</p><p>The most aggressive chemotherapy treatments often only provide patients minimal time, about four to six months. Chung went through six months of chemotherapy, then radiation and surgery. She was briefly disease-free, but then it came back — a typical and brutal reality with pancreatic cancer. </p><p>Soon after, she got into a clinical trial at the University of Chicago for a drug now considered to be the most promising treatment for pancreatic cancer — daraxonrasib. The treatment — not yet approved for use but nearing regulatory approval — is the first to considerably extend the lives of people with pancreatic cancer.</p><p>"It was pretty miraculous," Chung said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c70000" name="image-c70000"></a> <picture called the drug "revolutionary."</p><p>"This is going to change everything for pancreatic cancer," Shergill said. "Where we go from here is endless."</p><p>Daraxonrasib is a pill taken three times a day. The federal Food and Drug Administration recently granted Revolution Medicines, the company behind the drug, permission to give some patients access to the drug through a regulatory shortcut called expanded access.</p><p>The drug targets a mutation in pancreatic cancer cells that occurs in more than 90% of cases, Shergill said. </p><p>"That mutation is foundational to pancreatic cancer," Shergill said. "After a very long time, we have a pill that targets that mutation."</p><p>The method of targeting that mutation, called KRAS, is so promising that similar drugs targeting the mutation are <a class="Link" href="https://kras-kickers.github.io/krashub-web/index.html" target="_blank" ><u>being tested</u></a> for other cancers, including those of the lungs and colon.</p><p>People with metastatic pancreatic cancer who have "previously been treated" are eligible to receive the drug, <a class="Link" href="https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-permits-expanded-access-investigational-pancreatic-cancer-drug" target="_blank" ><u>according to the FDA</u></a>. The drug maker will provide it free — common practice with expanded access.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-portrait-right> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ardaman Shergill is an oncologist at the University of Chicago Medical Center. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Two recent clinical trials of the drug had the most encouraging results ever for a pancreatic-cancer treatment. Shergill oversaw the University of Chicago's participation in that <a class="Link" href="https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06625320" target="_blank" ><u>global study</u></a>. </p><p>People previously treated were randomly given daraxonrasib or a second round of a standard treatment. The experimental drug more than doubled survival rates. The survival rate with the standard chemotherapy treatment was six months. People who got the new drug got 13 more months of life, on average. </p><p>"It's not five to 10 years, but it's really great and more than double the standard treatment," Shergill said. "We're getting survivals at levels we haven't seen before." </p><p>The research is being presented this weekend at McCormick Place during a massive conference held by the American Society of Clinical Oncology.</p><p>The drug needs full approval from the FDA before it can be available to all patients. Shergill said she expects that will be by the end of this summer or the fall.</p><p>Since the FDA's decision to expand access, Shergill and others have been flooded with interest.</p><p>Chung, who used to work as a physician, was thrilled she was randomly assigned the drug. Taking a pill three times a day was far better than eight hours tied to a chemo IV drip. The side effects have been far more manageable than with chemo. She developed a rash that she's been able to get treated.</p><p>"Comparatively, it's been so much better," Chung said. "Well, first of all, I'm alive. Most treatments give you four to six months. And I've gotten a whole 'nother year."</p><p>Chung and her family traveled to Korea to visit relatives. She was able to help her daughter move into her college dorm in Boston and attend family weekend — something she missed out on when her twin sons headed to school because she was too sick.</p><p>The drug gave her time that chemotherapy couldn't, but it isn't a cure. Chung is well aware her extra time might be coming to an end. She started taking the drug last June.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b70000" entries.title: Witness heard 30 rifle rounds when FBI agents in riot gear shot convicted bank robber on West Side
entries.summary: <p>Tim Dunkin was relaxing, sitting outside his Garfield Park neighborhood home Thursday afternoon when he saw an SUV with its windows tinted suddenly get boxed in by three federal vehicles.</p><p>Within minutes, Dunkin heard at least 30 shots and saw FBI agents with riot shields and long guns navigating around the 3700 block of West Lexington Street, where they fatally shot Abdulhafedh H. Abdulhafedh, a 25-year-old man on parole for a bank robbery.</p><p>“I ain’t never seen nothing like that in my life,” Dunkin, 34, told the Sun-Times on Friday. </p><p>The hail of gunfire didn't last long. When the shots stopped, Dunkin grabbed his cell phone and began taking videos of the aftermath. </p><p>The block where the shooting occurred remained cordoned off by red and yellow crime scene tape Friday morning, and at least five FBI agents were present.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" scene, which happened around 3 p.m. Thursday, according to the Chicago Fire Department, the FBI and the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>Officials haven't released details about what led to the shooting.</p><p>The shooting happened about a block from John Milton Gregory Elementary School, where some students and staff were outside when shots rang out shortly, according to a note sent to parents and guardians. The school went on lockdown until CPD confirmed the situation had ended.</p><p>"Please know that we are taking this incident extremely seriously," Lateeya Toombs, principal at Gregory Elementary, said in the note. "I know situations like this can cause concern in our community; if your child voices any fears to you about what happened, please let us know so that we can give them extra support."</p><p>One man who stopped by the shooting scene Thursday said he was the dead man’s half-brother, but the man declined to give his name, saying he feared retaliation. </p><p>He said his half-brother had told him he’d been pulled over by federal agents earlier in the week. His half-brother, he added, had FaceTimed another one of their siblings as soon as he was pulled over Thursday, and was still talking to that sibling when the gunfire started.</p><p>Abdulhafedh had been released on parole Jan. 8 after being convicted of robbery of a financial institution, according to the Illinois Department of Corrections website.</p><p>Abdulhafedh was sentenced to four years behind bars for the crime, which was prosecuted out of Will County, according to the site.</p><p><i>Contributing: Violet Miller</i> </p>

entries.title: Alcalde Johnson y el papa León XIV hablan en Roma sobre la esclavitud, guerra y una invitación a Chicago
entries.summary: <p>CIUDAD DEL VATICANO — “¿Cómo está Chicago?”.</p><p>Esa fue la primera pregunta que le hizo el papa León XIV al alcalde de Chicago, Brandon Johnson, cuando se encontraron en una reunión privada el jueves por la tarde en el Vaticano.</p><p>Para Johnson, era claramente una pregunta pastoral.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8f0000" name="module-8f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>También se sentía la confianza, como si el papa estuviera preguntando: “¿Cómo está tu gente?”.</p><p>“Pude decir que Chicago es fuerte y que estamos transformándonos”, dijo Johnson durante una conferencia de prensa en la Universidad Americana de Roma poco después de reunirse durante más de 20 minutos a solas con el primer papa estadounidense nacido en Chicago. “Él hizo, creo, un gran gesto pastoral, un placer escuchar el increíble progreso que… hemos logrado”.</p><p>Durante su visita, Johnson le presentó al papa una carta formal de invitación, pidiéndole que por favor viniera a Chicago en 2027 para celebrar una misa, siguiendo los pasos de su predecesor, el papa Juan Pablo II, quien pasó dos días en Chicago en octubre de 1979. El primer papa polaco del mundo celebró una misa en Grant Park, atrayendo a una multitud de aproximadamente 1.5 millones de personas. [<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/05/28/pope-leo-grant-park-mass-invite-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" >Lee el texto de la carta.</a>]</p><p>“El 5 de octubre de 1979 se recordará para siempre como el día más espiritualmente inspirador en la historia de Chicago”, comenzaba la carta de invitación de Johnson a León. “Su santidad, usted era un joven sacerdote en formación en ese momento. Quizás estuvo allí. Quizás consideraría realizar una visita papal nuevamente casi 50 años después para compartir su propio mensaje de esperanza, unidad y servicio”.</p><p>Ha habido especulaciones en algunos sectores de que León XIV no visitaría Estados Unidos hasta que el presidente Donald Trump, con quien ha chocado públicamente, saliera del cargo. Pero Johnson insistió en que no escuchó ninguna vacilación por parte del papa en visitar su ciudad natal más temprano que tarde.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Y fue importante que Chicago lo abrazara, que lo bendijera, que oráramos por él porque sabemos que alguien de su importancia será un blanco. Así que oramos por su consuelo. durante su conversación privada en el Vaticano.</p><p>“Primero que nada, le agradecí por su valentía”, dijo Johnson. “Le agradecí por su postura moral contra estas guerras interminables y, ciertamente, hablé sobre el voto que emití en el Concejo Municipal hace un par de años, pidiendo un cese al fuego [en Gaza] y la liberación de rehenes, y sobre nuestra postura continua en favor del fin de estas guerras ilegales. También hablamos sobre elevar la conciencia sobre las condiciones que muchas personas están viviendo, ya sea en Chicago, Haití, Venezuela, Cuba.</p><p>“Hablamos sobre las condiciones que el legado prolongado de la esclavitud y la desinversión han tenido en la comunidad negra en Estados Unidos y en el mundo. Tuve una conversación con él sobre las reparaciones [para los descendientes de la esclavitud] y por qué es importante reparar el daño causado por el brutal legado de la esclavitud”, continuó Johnson.</p><p>“Intercambiamos aprecio por nuestras posturas en este momento, para hablar con los más vulnerables, para hablar con él sobre la asequibilidad… y nuevamente, continuar usando su púlpito así como yo usaré mi pluma, para llevar justicia a… la humanidad”.</p><p>Fue un encuentro entre dos hombres poderosos e influyentes, y para Johnson permanecerá como una experiencia profundamente espiritual.</p><p>“Cuando entras en la presencia de alguien de su magnitud, que camina e impregna el espíritu de nuestro Señor y Salvador, el momento en que dijo: ‘Toma asiento y únete a mí’, fue simplemente un intercambio pacífico de consuelo, de saber que así como el Espíritu Santo garantiza… siempre estamos confortados. Esa es la gracia y el amor que sentí de Su Santidad”.</p><p>Aproximadamente a las 4 p.m. en Roma, León XIV le dio la bienvenida a Johnson y a una delegación de más de 40 influyentes habitantes de Chicago de las comunidades empresariales, religiosas, educativas y cívicas de la ciudad.</p><p>Algunos se arrodillaron y le besaron el anillo, dijo Guy Chipparoni, presidente de Choose Chicago, la agencia de turismo y convenciones de la ciudad. Según Chipparoni, cuando Johnson invitó a León XIV a celebrar la misa en Chicago el próximo año, el papa pareció receptivo a la idea.</p><p>“Simplemente sonrió y dijo, ‘Me gustaría hacerlo’”, contó Chipparoni.</p><p>La delegación le presentó a “Da Pope” alrededor de dos docenas de regalos, la mayoría con temática de Chicago. [<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/05/28/pope-leo-chicago-gifts-list-vatican-cubs-hat-giardinara" target="_blank" >Lee una lista de todos los regalos que le dieron al papa.</a>]</p><p>Johnson le presentó a León XIV una llave de la ciudad, contándole sobre las personalidades que la habían recibido antes que él, incluidas Nelson Mandela, Herbie Hancock, el Reverendo Jesse Jackson y Frank Sinatra.</p><p>“Le dije, ‘No sé cuántas llaves tenga que usar para el Vaticano, pero solo hay una llave para Chicago’. Y nos alegramos de dársela”, bromeó Johnson.</p><p>Además de pasar tiempo a solas con el alcalde, el papa, de 70 años, originario del suburbio sur de Dolton, saludó a cada miembro de la delegación. Las visitas fueron breves —alrededor de un minuto cada una— pero la experiencia para muchos fue enriquecedora.</p><p>“Me acerqué y comencé a hablar y me emocioné”, dijo Robert Manuel, presidente de la Universidad DePaul. Fue su primera audiencia papal. León puso su brazo sobre el hombro de Manuel y lo miró a los ojos.</p><p>“Él dijo, ‘Está bien’, y eso me hizo emocionarme aún más”, dijo Manuel, con el sentimiento nuevamente en su expresión. “Esperaba que fuera mucho más formal y no tan íntimo y cercano”.</p><p>El regalo de Manuel en nombre de DePaul fueron copias de los diplomas que recibieron los padres de León XIV. Tanto su madre, Mildred, como su padre, Louis, fueron graduados de DePaul.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-16af69" name="image-16af69"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ecc64a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F99%2F91294086436b83f3da99ba811a5b%2Fmayorpopemeet-260528-02.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9aeb862/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F99%2F91294086436b83f3da99ba811a5b%2Fmayorpopemeet-260528-02.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dbb29a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2F99%2F91294086436b83f3da99ba811a5b%2Fmayorpopemeet-260528-02.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="El presidente de DePaul, Robert L. entries.title: Humboldt Park wedding videographer wins $20,000 grant from The Knot
entries.summary: <p>Humboldt Park wedding videographer Carlos Cedeno won $20,000 for his small business from The Knot, the online wedding platform announced Thursday. </p><p>Cedeno is the sole winner in Illinois among 26 small businesses nationwide, who were awarded a total of $500,000 from The Knot Worldwide’s inaugural small business grant program.</p><p>Other winners selected from more than 1,100 applications included wedding planners, photographers, florists and venues in 15 states.</p><p>Cedeno’s work is distinct because of his documentary-style wedding videos, modeled after reality TV shows.</p><p>“I’m obsessed with storytelling. I’m a story junkie,” he said.</p><p>Cedeno is self-taught and learned how to shoot and produce video in his 20s. Then someone asked him to shoot their wedding.</p><p>“I mic’d up almost the entire wedding party. I’m looking for moments that are unforgettable: Tears, the grandmother whispering how proud she is. After that, I caught the bug,” he said.</p><p>In 2019, he started his company Carlos C. Media. Since then, he has made about 100 wedding videos for clients mostly in the Chicago area. He has 36 weddings booked from this month through December, though summer is the busiest time.</p><p>Cedeno’s videos are 20 to 45 minutes and trailers are about a minute. He works across communities and ethnicities in English and Spanish. Clients find him on social media and word of mouth. His rates range from $4,000 to $10,000.</p><p>Making documentary-style wedding videos is labor-intensive. He learned the craft by analyzing reality TV shows and learning about audio and video equipment on YouTube.</p><p>For his videos, Cedeno interviews wedding party members several times before the big day.</p><p>“I know what challenges they face, what makes them strong. Before the wedding, I already have an idea of what I want to shoot,” Cedeno said. “I’m kind of nosy. That’s why I’m good at what I do.”</p><p>He records grooms preparing for the wedding and interviews bridesmaids, groomsmen and relatives. The result is personal and immersive videos. “People want authenticity,” he said.</p><p>Cedeno recalled one bride saying her military father wouldn’t want to talk to him. But “when I asked him about his baby girl, that guy was bawling. He was a big teddy bear,” he said.</p><p>Business has been steady, though it is slower these days, Cedeno said. Many <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2025/11/28/shoppers-wicker-park-sales-small-business-saturday" target="_blank" >small businesses</a> are struggling with higher costs, economic uncertainty and weak consumer confidence. Cedeno knows of two wedding photo and video studios in Chicago that have closed recently.</p><p>“It’s almost like a race to the cheapest vendor. Overall, everyone has taken a hit,” he said. “In this industry, you have to stand out.”</p><p>Cedeno will use his $20,000 grant to pay for his co-working space at 2112, a film, music and tech incubator near Old Irving Park. He's a sole proprietor but has five contractors and is training more people in his unique style.</p><p>The grant will help Cedeno also buy additional audio gear.</p><p>“The more people I get to mic up, the more stories I get to record,” he said. His clients “always want more.”</p><p>This year, The Knot’s WeddingPro Grant Program awarded one grand prize winner $50,000; five winners $20,000 each; 10 winners $10,000 each; and 10 winners received advertising grants on The Knot and WeddingWire.</p><p>There are 900,000 small businesses on The Knot’s global platform. “We consistently hear from our wedding professionals that access to capital is a barrier to getting started in the industry,” Raina Moskowitz, CEO of The Knot Worldwide, said in a news release.</p><p>The awards also include advertising support and mentorship. They give “access to both capital and critical support services such as mentorship and education that will enable small business owners to further grow and scale,” Moskowitz said.</p><p>More than half of small businesses in the wedding industry have fewer than 10 employees, according to The Knot.</p><p>The company is evaluating the grant program to decide whether to offer it again. Applications were open to all U.S. wedding professionals who run small businesses, have been in business for at least six months, generate revenue and earn at least 50% of sales from weddings.</p>

entries.title: Boy, 13, dies days after South Shore shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 13-year-old boy who was wounded in a shooting last week in South Shore died Thursday, according to Chicago police. </p><p>Deantwan McKeever, 13, was found in a gangway on May 21 in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/21/13-year-old-boy-shot-south-shore-coles-avenue" target="_blank" >8200 block of South Coles Avenue</a> around 2:50 p.m., police said.</p><p>Deantwan had been shot in the head and was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in critical condition. He was pronounced dead Thursday, the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>The day of the shooting, multiple witnesses heard two shots and saw surveillance footage of two males running past Deantwan's house around the time of the shooting, police said. A shell casing was found in a gangway near where the boy was found, according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>A car theft was happening around the same time and in the same area of the shooting, according to police reports.</p><p>No arrests have been made. <br></p>

entries.title: Man accused of killing Loyola University student caught with a shank while in custody
entries.summary: <p>A man accused of killing a Loyola University student was caught with a weapon while in custody at Cook County Jail. </p><p>Jose Medina, a 26-year-old Venezuelan immigrant, is facing first-degree murder, attempted murder and weapons charges. He’s accused of shooting Sheridan Gorman in the early hours of March 19 while she was on the lakefront in Rogers Park near the Loyola campus. </p><p>Gorman and some friends were walking toward the end of the pier a little after midnight at Tobey Prinz Beach when they spotted Medina hiding in the shadows, according to Cook County prosecutors.</p><p>Medina allegedly jumped out wearing a mask and holding a gun. He fired once as the group tried to run away, striking Gorman in her back and killing her. </p><p>Medina has been in custody since March 23. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div He’d made his way there after fleeing Venezuela.</p><p>Medina ended up in Chicago in 2023 after being detained at the U.S.-Mexico border in Texas. Though he asked to be deported back to Colombia, officials in Texas bused him to Chicago, according to his public defenders.</p><p>When he was arrested in connection to Gorman’s killing, Medina had an active warrant for a 2023 shoplifting case. Federal prosecutors also have charged Medina with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/02/chicago-crime-sheridan-gorman-loyola" target="_blank" >possessing a pistol</a> while being unlawfully present in the United States. entries.title: West Loop’s Smyth named No. 1 restaurant in North America
entries.summary: <p>Smyth, Chicago’s only three-Michelin-starred restaurant, was named the No. 1 restaurant in North America on Thursday.</p><p>Last year, the West Loop restaurant won the No. 4 spot at the inaugural <a class="Link" href="https://www.theworlds50best.com/stories/News/north-americas-50-best-restaurants-2026-1-50-list.html" target="_blank" ><u>Best Restaurants in North America</u></a> ceremony, hosted by <a class="Link" href="https://www.theworlds50best.com/" target="_blank" ><u>50 Best</u></a>. Smyth is the sole restaurant from Chicago on this year’s list. The accolade comes ahead of the New American establishment’s 10th anniversary in August.</p><p>The restaurant’s executive chef, John Shields, and his wife Karen Urie-Shields, a pastry chef, are the power couple behind the restaurant. The Shields couldn’t be reached for comment on Friday as they traveled back to Chicago, but John Shields said in a press release that they were “deeply honored” to be named this year’s best restaurant in North America. He added that the award also belongs to their team, partner and diners.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a
